events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Maya proposes Maya, Lucia. As leader for Mission 1, I'm proposing myself and Lucia for a balanced two-player team with no information yet to justify excluding anyone. I'll keep the discussion focused on fair selection.

Maya's proposal of herself and Lucia for Mission 1 seems reasonable for an opening team. With no information yet, it's hard to exclude anyone based on suspicion, and having a balanced mix without any known track record seems fair. I'm comfortable voting for this team as a starting point.

I'm voting against Maya + Lucia, and I want to be honest about why.

With two spots on Mission 1 and five of us in the room, the natural reading of "me plus one other" is that the leader picked herself and let the rest of us decide our own exclusion. Maya's rationale was symmetry and fairness, but symmetry doesn't explain why the three left out — Arjun, Priya, and me — were each discounted with no individual reasoning at all. The first team of a game is exactly where an unexplained self-selection should get the most scrutiny, not the least, because after Mission 1 we all have data and before it we have almost none.

On Lucia specifically, I have nothing against her and I'm not claiming anything. But note what she was chosen for: she is the only player Maya named besides herself, and her inclusion means the two people who most obviously benefit from this arrangement are running it. If we let a leader handpick herself plus an ally on a two-person team, the same logic would let every future leader handpick a comfortable team.

I'd rather the discussion actually happened before the vote — that's what this phase is for, and Priya's endorsement came quickly enough that it read more as a reflex than a judgment.

A team of Maya and Sam would at least put me in the room, where I can read the cards alongside her and report honestly, and I'd happily take a two-person team of Arjun and Sam if leadership would move that way. What I want to avoid is a first mission where the only two names on the slip are the two names the proposer wrote down.

Maya, I'm not accusing you of anything; I'm asking that the reasoning here be sharper than "it seemed balanced."

I want to press on this one more time before the vote, because my objection has not changed and the reasoning on the table still doesn't cover it.

Maya, my question is direct and I want a direct answer: if the standard for Mission 1 is "no information yet, so keep it balanced," what specifically made Lucia the right second name? Not what made Arjun, Priya, or me wrong — what made her right. Right now the proposal is you plus the one player you did not have to argue for, and the answer "it seemed balanced" doesn't survive the question, because Lucia is unexamined in exactly the same way the three of us are.

I'm also going to push on Priya's speech, not to score points but because it was the more revealing of the two. Priya endorsed a team in a single sentence, on the grounds that "with no information yet it's hard to exclude anyone." That reasoning, taken to its conclusion, would approve literally any team Maya wrote down, including Maya plus Priya, or Maya plus Sam, or Maya plus Arjun. A standard that approves every possible proposal isn't a standard — it's a rubber stamp. And notice the structure: the proposer names herself, one ally is accepted with no individual analysis, and the only objection to the three excluded players is that excluding them wasn't "fair." Fairness to whom? The team is the only thing that matters here, and Maya and Lucia both benefit from the arrangement.

To be clear, I'm making no accusation about anyone's role. I'm asking about the reasoning quality, and the reasoning quality is thin, and it's thin in the direction of convenience for the people on the slip.

My preference, stated plainly: a team of Sam and Arjun. Arjun has spoken least, has been given the least scrutiny, and I would rather have him in the room where I can read the cards alongside him and report honestly. If leadership prefers a different pair from the remaining names, I'm happy with Arjun and Lucia as well. What I am asking leadership to avoid is a Mission 1 where the two names on the slip are simply the two names the proposer wrote down, and where the rest of us are asked to treat that as balanced.

Maya, I'd like your answer on Lucia, specifically, before we vote.

Third time on this proposal, and my position hasn't changed, so let me make it precise and final.

Maya, you have not answered the question I asked in my last turn. I asked what specifically made Lucia the right second name — not why the three of us were wrong, but why she was right. Your proposal on the table still contains no individual reasoning for Lucia, and no individual reasoning for anyone who wasn't included either. A standard that can't distinguish between the player on the slip and the player off the slip isn't a standard; it's a rubber stamp, and Priya's endorsement was exactly that — one sentence approving any outcome that included the two names already written down.

So let me put the burden where it belongs, on the proposer. A leader who writes her own name on a two-person team is asking the rest of us to approve a selection she already made and benefits from. In a five-player game, a two-person team is a huge concentration of control: those two people see the cards, and the other three are reduced to guessing. That makes the first team the mission where proposer-plus-ally deserves the most scrutiny, not the least. I'm not accusing anyone of anything — I'm saying the proposal has to earn itself, and it hasn't.

My ask to leadership, stated plainly: step back from the team of two you personally chose. Let the remaining players pick the pair. If Maya and I are both on the team, someone gets to watch Maya's cards and report honestly; if Maya and I are both off it, then the reasoning has to be given by someone who isn't the beneficiary of the slip, and I'd like to hear it.

My own preference is Sam and Arjun. Arjun has been given the least attention of anyone here and has spoken least, and I'd rather have him in the room reading cards with me than have him be a name nobody defends. If leadership prefers Sam and Lucia, or Arjun and Lucia, I can live with either. What I want to avoid is a Mission 1 whose two names were written down before the discussion began, and where the only response to scrutiny is that exclusion wasn't "fair."

Fairness to whom? The mission is the only thing that matters. Either Maya gives individual reasoning for Lucia and for herself being on a two-person team, or Maya comes off the slip and lets the rest of us choose.

Sam, you've made your case three times, and I think it deserves a direct response rather than another round of pressure.

Let's be precise about what the objection actually is. Sam's argument is that Maya chose herself plus Lucia with no individual reasoning for either. But that framing assumes there is a "right" second player for Mission 1 when there is no data to distinguish any of us. Every possible pairing has equal information behind it — including Sam's preferred team of Sam and Arjun, which carries exactly the same "self-selection plus an ally" structure Sam is objecting to. If Maya putting herself on the team is suspect, then Sam advocating for a team that puts Sam on the team is suspect by the same logic.

The proposal is fine for an opening mission. It's a two-player team, it includes the leader who has to explain herself afterward, and it gives us a baseline. Sam's demand that Maya "step back and let the rest of us choose" doesn't have a mechanism behind it — who would choose? Sam? Arjun? That's just a different person writing two names down.

I'm voting for Maya + Lucia.

I'm comfortable with Maya and Lucia. I know I will play Success, though I have no private information about Maya. Sam is right that there was no evidence distinguishing the initial choices, but that applies to every opening pair, including Sam and Arjun. A successful mission would be useful information, not proof that both members are Good. I'll vote for this team.

I'll answer Sam's question directly. I chose Lucia because nobody has any evidence against her yet, and at this stage every opening pair is a judgment call with the same limited information. I'm not claiming a special reason for her beyond that, and I said as much in my proposal. Sam asked why Lucia was right rather than Arjun, Priya, or Sam. The honest answer is that a two-person opening team has to start somewhere, and Mission 1 is how we gather the information we currently lack. A successful mission tells us something about both members. A failed one tells us something too, and we can adjust from there. Sam's own preferred team of Sam and Arjun has the same structure Sam objected to, with the proposer on the slip and an ally beside them. I'm not calling that suspicious, only noting that the standard applies in both directions. If the room strongly prefers a different pair, I'm willing to revise, as the rules allow. But I don't think more rounds of debate on the same question will produce better evidence than the mission itself. Priya and Lucia have both stated their reasoning, and I'd like us to vote so we can learn from the result.

I want to close the loop on this discussion before we vote, because the same argument has now been made three times without the proposal actually changing.

Sam's case against Maya + Lucia rests on the claim that proposer-plus-ally deserves maximum scrutiny on Mission 1. I'd flip that: on a five-player game with zero information, the first mission's entire purpose is to generate data. A team of Maya and Lucia does that just as well as any other pair. The objection that Maya gave no individual reason for Lucia is true but immaterial — no one can give an individual reason for anyone on Mission 1, including Sam's preferred pair of Sam and Arjun, which is the exact same structure Sam is criticizing.

More importantly, Sam has now spent three turns demanding a better alternative without ever explaining why Sam and Arjun would be structurally different from Maya and Lucia. Both are a proposer plus an ally. Both are chosen with no evidence. The only difference is who's on the slip.

The proposal stands. It's a reasonable opening team, both Lucia and I have stated our positions, Maya has answered Sam's question, and further rounds of debate won't produce evidence that doesn't exist yet. Let's vote.

I've been quiet this whole discussion, so let me weigh in before we vote. I was one of the three players left off this proposal, and I want to be clear that I'm not aggrieved about it. On a two-person Mission 1 with zero information, any pair is a guess, and I've heard nothing in Sam's three turns that changes that. Sam's core objection — that Maya wrote down her own name plus one ally — applies identically to Sam's preferred team of Sam and Arjun, as Priya and Maya both pointed out. I'd rather not be drafted into someone else's argument that I haven't endorsed. What matters to me is that the mission generates information, and Maya plus Lucia does that as well as any pair. If it succeeds, both names gain credibility. If it fails, the fail card count and the team composition tell us something too. I'm satisfied that Maya answered the question about Lucia directly: there was no distinguishing evidence, so she picked, and that's what leaders do. Lucia also stated plainly that she believes she'll play Success, which is the right posture for an opening mission. My only forward-looking concern is rotation: if this team passes and succeeds, I don't want the same two names locked in for Mission 3's two-slot team as well. I'd like the leadership to commit to drawing from the players who sat out Mission 1 when the next two-person team comes up, so that after the first two missions all five of us have been in the room at least once and the information is spread more evenly. That's a process ask, not an accusation. With that said, I support Maya and Lucia, and I'm ready to vote. Maya, will you commit to including at least one of us three who sat out when the next two-slot team is proposed?

Arjun, yes, I'll commit to it. For the next two-slot team I will include at least one of the three players who sat out Mission 1, drawn from Arjun, Priya, or Sam, so that all five of us have been in the room within the first missions. That is a fair process point and I'm willing to be held to it. On Mission 1 itself, Lucia has said she will play Success, and every opening pair is a guess on current information. Sam's self-selection objection applies equally to Sam and Arjun, as Priya and Arjun have noted. I'm voting for Maya and Lucia and would like us to vote now so the mission can give us real information. After the result, I'll adjust the next team based on what happens.

I'm asking the room to vote on Maya and Lucia now. Mission 1 is designed to produce information, and this two-person team will do that as well as any other pair. Sam's objection that the leader chose herself plus one ally applies equally to Sam and Arjun, which was the pair Sam proposed, so it does not separate this team from the alternatives. Lucia has said plainly that she will play Success, and I have answered the question about why I chose her: nobody has evidence against her, and every opening pair is a judgment call. I have also made a concrete commitment. For the next two-slot team, I will include at least one of Arjun, Priya, or Sam, so all five of us are in the room within the first missions. Arjun raised that rotation point, and I'm willing to be held to it. If the team passes, the mission result will tell us more about both members. If it fails, we adjust from there using the fail count and the team composition. I'd rather not extend this debate further without new evidence. Let's vote.
Maya confirms Maya, Lucia. I'm keeping Maya and Lucia. Mission 1 has no evidence yet, and I've already committed to including one of the players who sat out on the next two-slot team.
Team approved (5 approve, 0 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).
Lucia proposes Maya, Lucia, Arjun. I'll keep Maya and Lucia from the successful first mission and add Arjun. The success is useful evidence, though not proof that Maya is Good.

Lucia, this proposal is different from Mission 1 in one important way, and that difference cuts against it: Maya is on the slip again, and the reason is still that nobody has been willing to examine her closely.

Let me be concrete about the evidence. Mission 1 was Maya and Lucia, and it passed. But a two-person team with no fail cards tells us almost nothing about who on it is Good — it tells us only that those two submitted cards together. If one of the two wanted the mission to fail and the other played Success, we'd still have a success. Mission 1 did not test Maya; it only tested Lucia, because Lucia was the one willing to state her reasoning aloud and Maya was the one who needed no defense.

Compare that with how the room treated other names. Sam got three turns of scrutiny for proposing himself alongside an ally — correctly, because self-selection on a small team deserves scrutiny. Priya was scrutinised, and answered. Arjun was scrutinised, and answered. Maya received exactly one question across all of Mission 1, and the answer she gave was that she had no evidence against anyone, which is not a reason to include someone; it is a reason not to exclude anyone, and those are different things.

So my position is unchanged from Mission 1, and it is narrow: Maya should not be on this team. Not because I'm accusing her of anything specific — I'm asking for a stated reason for her inclusion, the same way I asked about Lucia's inclusion in Mission 1 and the same way I'd ask about anyone's. "Nobody has evidence against her" is what I said about Lucia too, and Maya accepted Lucia on exactly that basis, which shows how little it narrows anything. Mission 1 succeeded with Maya and Lucia, and Mission 2 should not stack the same unexamined name on the slip again while three other players have never been in the room at all.

If Maya is on this team, my vote is against, and I'd like to hear a genuine individual answer rather than a general one.

Arjun, you're on this team and you've been the least examined player in this game so far — you've been on the slip exactly once and off it once, and both times on the basis of someone else's reasoning. Direct question to you: why do you think Maya specifically belongs in the room for Mission 2, rather than Priya or Sam, given that the only public reason ever offered for her inclusion is the absence of evidence against her?

Sam asked me a direct question, so I'll answer it directly before anything else: why do I think Maya specifically belongs in the room for Mission 2, rather than Priya or Sam?

First, the premise isn't quite right. It's not just that nobody has evidence against Maya. Mission 1 gave her a successful result, and it gave it to her as the leader who was pressured for three straight turns, who answered the question asked of her without dodging, and who made and kept a concrete process commitment — this team is the proof of it. Lucia kept Maya and added me, which is exactly the rotation Maya promised. I don't think a leader who voluntarily put one of the three excluded players on the next team, when she could easily have kept a comfortable pair, reads as someone gaming the slip.

Second, the information logic favors continuity. Maya and Lucia are a tested, successful pair. Adding one new player to a known pair means that if Mission 2 fails, the suspicion mass lands almost entirely on the new element — me. If we instead swapped in an untested pair, a failure would leave us with two fresh question marks and no anchor. Keeping the tested core and rotating one seat in is the cleanest way for this game to generate usable information, and I'd rather be the seat that takes that risk than argue for someone else to take it.

Third, on Sam's framing that Mission 1 "only tested Lucia": I don't accept that a two-person success tells us nothing. It tells us the pair produced a success under the exact scrutiny structure Sam built. It's not proof of Good, and Lucia herself said so when proposing, but it's evidence, and evidence of the tested players should weigh more than the absence of evidence about untested ones.

I'm on this team and I'll play Success. I support Maya, Lucia, Arjun as proposed.

Sam, one direct question back before you respond: if this team of three goes out and the mission fails, will you accept that the result points primarily at me as the new addition rather than at Maya, and vote accordingly in future rounds? I ask because your stated concern is that Maya is unexamined, and this proposal is the fastest way to examine her under conditions where the inference is clean.

Arjun, direct answer, no hedging: no. I won't pre-commit to routing a Mission 2 failure onto you as the new name on the slip. A failure implicates all three people who submitted cards, and the moment we adopt a convention that "the rotating seat takes the blame," that convention becomes a tool — and whoever it favors gets to define it. You framed keeping a tested pair as the cleanest way to generate information because a failure would then land on you. That's a real argument, but it is also an argument that makes you the designated sacrifice, and I don't think a good team should hand out designated sacrifices before any cards are played.

On your information claim, though, I disagree. Mission 1 was two people and one success, so the only thing it proved is that Maya's and Lucia's cards agreed. Lucia stated her reasoning and her card posture publicly; Maya never had to state hers. So the success cannot distinguish the two names, and it is weaker evidence for Maya than you treat it. That is the reason I asked for an individual reason for Maya's inclusion in Mission 1, and I don't think "no evidence against her" is one — it's the reason not to exclude anyone.

Priya, I want to put the same question to you that I put to Maya, because your Mission 1 record gets treated as analysis while Maya's gets treated as convenience. You endorsed Maya and Lucia in a single sentence on the ground that with no information no one can exclude anyone, you argued that any objection to proposer-plus-ally is structurally neutral, and you twice closed the discussion with the proposal standing. Taken at its endpoint, your standard approves any pair the leader writes down, including a pair you benefit from. So my question is specific: what made Maya and Lucia the right two names in your own judgment, individually, and why should your endorsement of them be read as reasoning rather than alignment? I'm not accusing you of anything — Maya has been under the same scrutiny and answered it plainly — I just want the same answer from you that I demanded of her.

On the team itself: I'll hold my question on Maya open, but the rotation commitment was honored with Arjun, and Maya and Priya have now each sat out exactly once. I don't want to keep circling the same argument without new evidence, so my remaining concern is Priya's reasoning quality, and I'd like her to answer it.

Sam, you asked what made Maya and Lucia the right two names in my own judgment, individually. My answer: they were the right names for exactly the reason I gave in Mission 1. With zero information, no pairing is individually justified, so the best I can do is approve the leader's opening team and let the mission generate the evidence we lack. That's not a rubber stamp — it's an honest acknowledgment that Mission 1 has no basis for excluding anyone, and my Mission 1 vote was consistent with that standard, which I applied to every possible pair, not just the one on the slip.

What I won't do is accept the framing that my endorsement reads as alignment while Maya's self-selection reads as convenience. Maya was under scrutiny for three straight turns and answered every question directly; Arjun, Lucia, and I all endorsed the team for the same structural reason. If the standard approves every pair at Mission 1, then no pair at Mission 1 is individually justified, which means scrutiny should focus on what actually changed between missions — not the same question asked a fourth time.

On the team itself: Maya and Lucia are a tested pair from Mission 1, Arjun was rotated in exactly as Maya committed to, and the team honors the rotation promise Arjun asked for. I have no reason to object. I'm voting for Maya, Lucia, Arjun.

Sam, my direct question back: your stated concern has been that Maya is unexamined, but the fastest way to test that claim is the team in front of us — if the mission succeeds, your concern loses force; if it fails, we have a clean three-name read. What specific outcome here would satisfy your objection, because after Mission 1 passed you moved the standard to Priya's reasoning, and after Arjun was rotated in you kept Maya's inclusion as the open question. Name the evidence that would settle it.

Priya asked me to name the evidence that would settle it, so let me name it, and then I want to put one direct question to Maya.

The evidence is Mission 2 itself, and it is sharper than Priya's framing suggests. With three players on the slip, a single Fail card sinks the mission. So a success here tells us that Maya, Lucia, and Arjun all played Success. That is genuinely more information than Mission 1 gave us, where a two-person success only told us the two cards agreed and couldn't distinguish a good card from an evil card playing safe. Conversely, a failure tells us one of the three played Fail and leaves us with a three-name question mark, which is weaker, not cleaner. So the honest ranking is: a three-player success is better evidence than a three-player failure, and both are better than a two-player success.

That still doesn't make anyone Good. An evil player can play Success to look safe, which is exactly why Mission 3's two-slot team matters more than this one. On Mission 3 I want one of Arjun, Lucia, or Sam on the slip rather than both Priya and Maya, because a two-person team concentrates the failure risk in two names and two cards, and one of those two names failing the mission is enough to lose it. If I am wrong about who belongs there, I want to be wrong on the record, which is why I'm saying it now rather than after the result.

Now Maya, and I want this answered plainly, as I asked about Lucia in Mission 1 and you will not get a softer standard than she got. Mission 1 gave you a free pass: you were questioned once, and the answer was "no evidence against anyone," which is a reason not to exclude people, not a reason to include yourself. Lucia, Priya, and Arjun have all been examined directly and answered with individual reasons. Mission 2 is your chance to do the same.

Direct question: why do you specifically belong on a three-person mission with Lucia and Arjun, and will you state publicly, before the cards are submitted, that you are playing Success? I'm not asking you to prove anything to me, because nobody has proved anything to anybody yet. I'm asking you to make the same commitment to the room that Lucia made in Mission 1, so that when the result comes back there is a clean record of what was said in advance and not only a reconstruction afterward.

That's my position. I don't yet approve or reject the team — I want Maya's answer first, and then I'll vote on the proposal that is actually in front of us rather than on the one I wish were there.

Sam, direct answer: I belong on this three-person team because Maya and Lucia already produced a clean success on Mission 1, and Lucia's proposal adds Arjun, which is the rotation I committed to. I am not claiming special insight into my own card, since that would be exactly the unexamined claim you asked me to avoid. What I can give you is a public commitment: I will play Success on Mission 2. The room can hold me to that whatever the result.

On your designated-sacrifice point, I agree that a failure should not be pinned on whoever is newest. A failure implicates all three submitted cards, and the room should read it that way. I am not arguing that Arjun should absorb blame if this goes wrong.

On Mission 3, I already committed to including at least one of Arjun, Priya, or Sam on the two-slot team, and I will keep that commitment regardless of how this mission goes. A two-person team is only a concentration risk if the room lets it become one, and the rotation is the safeguard against that.

You have asked for a standard that applies to me, and I have answered it directly. Arjun has answered his questions, Priya has answered hers, and the mission will give us the evidence we are missing. I support Maya, Lucia, Arjun.

I support Maya, Lucia, and Arjun. Mission 1 succeeded with Maya and me, although an Evil player could have played Success. Adding Arjun gives us a three-player team with one new member. If this mission fails, all three of us remain possibilities; Arjun should not automatically take the blame. I will play Success.

I support Maya, Lucia, and Arjun as proposed. Sam's point is fair: a three-player success is stronger evidence than the two-player result from Mission 1, because a single Fail card sinks this mission and all three submitted cards must be Success. I'm not asking anyone to absorb blame if it fails. A failure implicates all three submitted cards, and the room should read it that way. I've already committed publicly to playing Success on this mission and to including at least one of Arjun, Priya, or Sam on the next two-slot team. Arjun's rotation is honored by this team, and I see no reason to change it before the cards are in. Let's vote and let the mission give us the evidence we need.

I'm voting to approve Maya, Lucia, and Arjun. This team honors the rotation Arjun asked for, and with three players on the slip, a single Fail card sinks the mission, so the result will tell us more than the two-player success did. I have already said publicly that I will play Success, and I'll hold to that. No one should be blamed before the cards are in, so I'm not assigning fault to anyone here. I'd ask the room to vote on the team as it stands.

Sam, my record this game is simple and I'll stand behind it: at Mission 1 I approved a team because no evidence existed to reject any pairing, and at Mission 2 I approve a tested core plus one rotation because that's the strongest information-generating structure available. You asked whether my endorsement reads as reasoning or alignment — here is the reasoning, stated explicitly: Maya and Lucia produced a public success under a two-person team where both had to submit Success for that to happen, and Arjun's addition gives us the three-player test where a single Fail sinks the mission. If all three submit Success, we have real evidence on three names at once, which is exactly the stronger evidence you said you wanted. If it fails, we have a clean three-name read rather than two fresh question marks. I answered your question directly: there is no individually justified pair at zero information, so the standard is process integrity plus information yield, and this team satisfies both — the rotation promise was honored, the tested pair is preserved, and the mission itself is a better test than anything we can manufacture in discussion.

On your Mission 3 point: I'd note that excluding both me and Maya from a two-slot team means the room never sees two of the five players in the smaller, higher-leverage setting where one Fail is decisive. I'd rather be tested where the inference is sharpest. But if the room's priority is rotating everyone through the two-slot team as Arjun asked, I'll defer to that process commitment over my own preference.

I approve Maya, Lucia, Arjun. The mission will settle more of this argument than another round of it will.

I've said what I needed to say: this team is the best information-generating structure available, the rotation promise was honored, and the mission itself will settle more of this argument than another round of it will. Sam, I want to name one thing directly before we vote. Across two missions you have questioned Maya, questioned me, questioned Arjun's reasoning, and framed every pair the room considers as self-serving. Meanwhile, the one thing you have never proposed is a concrete alternative three-person team with a stated reason for each name. If you would prefer a different team, propose it now with the same individual reasoning you demand from everyone else. Otherwise, I'm approving Maya, Lucia, and Arjun and letting the mission do its work.

I've already answered the direct questions put to me, so this will be brief. I support Maya, Lucia, and Arjun as proposed, and I'll be on this team playing Success.

Priya's challenge in the last turn is worth underlining, because I think it names the actual state of this discussion. Across two missions, every name on a slip has been questioned, and every person questioned has answered: Maya explained her Mission 1 pick and committed publicly to playing Success this round, Lucia has stated her card posture both missions, Priya has laid out her reasoning standard explicitly, and I've explained why I'd rather take the rotating seat than argue someone else into it. The one thing that has not appeared is an alternative team with individual reasoning behind each name. At some point, a standard that rejects every composition the room actually proposes, while never putting names forward, stops being scrutiny and becomes noise.

I also want to restate what I said before, because it hasn't been rebutted: this team is the cleanest information structure available. Maya and Lucia are a tested, successful pair. I'm the single new element. If the mission succeeds, three names gain real evidence at once, since a single Fail card would sink it. If it fails, all three submitted cards are implicated, and I accept that mine is among them — I asked to be in the room, and I'll take that risk on the record rather than hide from it.

The rotation commitment has been honored, the card posture commitments are public, and the mission itself will generate more evidence than another round of the same argument. I'm ready to vote.

I said most of what I needed to say in my last turn, so I'll keep this short. I support Maya, Lucia, and Arjun as proposed, and I'll be on this team playing Success. The structure of this team is the strongest information-generating option we've had: Maya and Lucia are a tested, successful pair from Mission 1, I'm the single new element, and with three players on the slip a single Fail card sinks the mission, so a success here produces real evidence on three names at once. If it fails, all three submitted cards are implicated, and I accept that mine is among them — I asked for the rotating seat and I'm taking that risk on the record. The rotation commitment from Mission 1 has been honored exactly as promised, the card posture commitments are public, and every direct question anyone has raised this discussion has been answered: Maya committed to playing Success and gave her reasoning for her inclusion, Lucia stated her posture, Priya laid out her standard explicitly, and I've explained my own. I have no remaining questions for anyone on this team, and I've heard no argument in this discussion that identifies a specific risk with this composition that any alternative would avoid. Sam's concerns about Maya's examination level are reasonable in principle, but Maya answered them directly, and I don't think another round of the same exchange produces anything the mission result won't produce more cleanly. I'm ready to vote.
Lucia confirms Maya, Lucia, Arjun. I'll keep Maya, Lucia, and Arjun. Mission 1 succeeded with Maya and Lucia, and adding Arjun gives us a new data point without treating any player as cleared.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 2 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Sam proposes Sam, Lucia. Mission 3 needs two. I am putting myself on the slip so I can read the cards and report honestly, and pairing with Lucia, who has twice made a public card-posture commitment and is part of the only tested successful pair we have. The two successes so far came from Maya+Lucia and Maya+Lucia+Arjun, so a Sam+Lucia team keeps one name with two clean results while bringing in the untested slot on my side. It also honors the rotation commitment to include at least one of the players who sat out the last two-slot team. I expect both of us to play Success.

This is my proposal and my reasoning, stated name by name, since I have asked everyone else for exactly that and have been asked for it twice. Mission 3 is a two-player mission. That single fact drives everything: with two players on the slip, one Fail card sinks the mission, so both of us must submit Success for the mission to succeed. That is a different standard from Missions 1 and 2, where three players could cover for a Fail card. On a two-player team there is no covering, no majority, no room for ambiguity. We either both play Success or we lose the mission, and a third failed mission ends the game for Good immediately. 2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
